Hunt & HackettIncident report

One phished mailbox became domain admin in 41 hours

Nothing in the path was an exploit. Every step used something that was already allowed.

A test fixture. Names and timings are invented.

The intruder never broke in twice

A stolen session opened a mailbox, the mailbox delivered a document, and each machine handed over the credential for the next. The sections below follow the path one hop at a time, with the evidence for each.

Five hops from a mailbox to the domain controller

Read on: the diagram follows the step you are reading.

Hour 0. A session is stolen

A fake sign-in page relays the login and keeps the session cookie. The finance clerk sees nothing unusual.

Hour 2. A colleague opens a document

It arrives from a real mailbox, so nobody doubts it. The macro starts a remote-access tool.

Hour 32. An administrator signs in

The intruder has waited on the workstation for this credential, and takes it from memory.

Hour 38. A password is found in a script

The backup account has not changed it in years.

Hour 41. The directory is theirs

The account can request a ticket for any service.

Any one of three controls would have ended it

Binding sessions to the device, keeping administrators off workstations, or alerting on new service tickets for old accounts would each have stopped the path at a different hop.
